Agents can pay. Mandate lets them prove they were allowed to.

An open-source accountability layer for AI-agent purchases on PayPal: you sign what your agent may buy, plain code checks every purchase against it before money moves, and a disputed payment is answered from evidence and published rules.

The problem

An AI agent with a payment method is a confused deputy. A line of text in a product review can talk it into spending someone's money, and when that payment is disputed nobody can show what the person actually allowed or who is at fault.

What Mandate does

  • Prove. You sign a Verifiable Intent credential chain. The PayPal order carries the hash of that chain, and receipts are signed.
  • Protect. A guard in plain code checks the chain, every limit, the merchant, the cart and a budget ledger. A quarantined extractor keeps web text away from the planner.
  • Resolve. A dispute agent applies a published rule set, assembles an evidence packet and decides refund, defend or human, with a money gate.
  • Attribute. Fault is split between the user, the agent platform and the merchant by deterministic rules. A model may explain the result; it cannot change it.

The rule that holds it together: the model proposes, code disposes. Money only moves through a gateway that demands a token the guard issues.

What is real and what is simulated

Nothing is oversold here. PayPal is an in-process simulator unless sandbox credentials are set, dispute outcomes are scripted, and the benchmark uses synthetic scenarios. The guard, ledger, credentials, liability rules, receipts and audit log are real code in every mode.

Where to go next

  • Try the buyer app: sign a mandate and send an agent shopping.
  • Open the merchant console: orders, guard decisions, disputes, audit log, benchmark.
  • Read the API reference, including the MCP endpoint for other agents.
  • Get in touch with questions or feedback.
